title: Cost-effectiveness of respiratory syncytial virus vaccines in post-marketing settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections, hospitalizations, and deaths, particularly among infants and older adults worldwide. This study aims to summarize cost-effectiveness evidence by pooling incremental net benefit (INB) estimates of marketed RSV vaccines.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: In this review, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through November 20, 2025. Grey literature and reference lists were also searched. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted separately for older adults and infants. Potential sources of heterogeneity were explored using population-specific subgroup analyses and univariable meta-regressions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Of the 17 studies included in the systematic review, 11 contributed to the primary meta-analysis and one additional study to sensitivity analysis only. Among older adults, the pooled INB was USD 105.05 [95% confidence interval (CI): USD 41.89–168.21; I2 = 93.2%]. For infants, the pooled INB was USD 5.81 (95% CI: USD −35.44–47.07; I2 = 89.4%). In the European subgroup, the pooled INB among older adults was USD 123.63 (95% CI: USD 41.23–206.02; I2 = 89.4%), while that for infants was USD 15.00 (95% CI: USD −4.33–34.34; I2 = 43.4%).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses showed robust pooled INBs among older adults, whereas infant estimates were sensitive to study exclusion. Substantial between-study heterogeneity warrants cautious interpretation of the pooled estimates and highlights the need to consider local epidemiology and implementation conditions when developing RSV vaccination policies.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Descriptive findings suggested that age- and risk-based targeting in older adults and seasonal maternal vaccination may yield higher INB estimates.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses the cost-effectiveness of RSV vaccines in post-marketing settings, focusing on older adults and infants. The review pooled incremental net benefit (INB) estimates from 17 studies, with 11 contributing to the primary meta-analysis and one to sensitivity analysis. For older adults, the pooled INB was USD 105.05 (95% CI: USD 41.89–168.21; I2 = 93.2%), indicating potential cost-effectiveness. For infants, the pooled INB was USD 5.81 (95% CI: USD −35.44–47.07; I2 = 89.4%), with results being sensitive to study exclusion. The European subgroup showed higher INB for older adults (USD 123.63; 95% CI: USD 41.23–206.02; I2 = 89.4%) and moderate INB for infants (USD 15.00; 95% CI: USD −4.33–34.34; I2 = 43.4%). Sensitivity analyses revealed robust findings for older adults but variability for infants. The review emphasizes the importance of local epidemiology and implementation conditions in RSV vaccination policy development. Age- and risk-based targeting in older adults and seasonal maternal vaccination may enhance cost-effectiveness.

title: RSV bronchiolitis admissions in infants immunized with nirsevimab: a multicenter observational study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of RSV bronchiolitis admissions following successful nationwide implementation of nirsevimab.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a retrospective multicenter study across 15 Spanish pediatric emergency departments during the 2024-2025 RSV season. Infants eligible for the RSV prophylaxis, defined as those younger than six months at the start of or during the RSV season, with laboratory-confirmed RSV bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization were included. Patients immunized fewer than seven days before admission or with unknown immunization status were excluded.
analysis.methods: Epidemiological and clinical data were analyzed according to nirsevimab status, with age-stratified and multivariable analyses performed.
analysis.main_results: Among 366 hospitalized infants with RSV bronchiolitis, 345 were previously healthy. Of these, 165/345 (47.8%) had received nirsevimab. Breakthrough cases were younger than non-breakthrough cases (2.0 months [IQR, 1.1-3.6] vs 5.2 months [IQR, 3.3-6.6]; p < 0.001). Overall, immunized and non-immunized infants showed similar rates of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission (26.7% vs 21.1%; p = 0.2) and length of hospital stay (5 days [IQR, 3-7] vs 5 days [IQR, 4-7]; p = 0.6).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that, once hospitalization is required, nirsevimab may offer limited additional protection against severe disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform future studies on the effectiveness of nirsevimab in preventing severe RSV disease and guide public health strategies for RSV prophylaxis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: After age stratification, clinical characteristics and outcomes remained comparable between groups. In multivariable analyses, no statistically significant association was observed between nirsevimab immunization and PICU admission, advanced respiratory support, or length of hospital stay.

analysis.summary_en: This multicenter observational study evaluated the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of RSV bronchiolitis admissions in infants immunized with nirsevimab during the 2024-2025 RSV season in Spain. The study included infants younger than six months with laboratory-confirmed RSV bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization, excluding those immunized fewer than seven days before admission or with unknown immunization status. Results showed that 47.8% of previously healthy hospitalized infants had received nirsevimab, and breakthrough cases were younger than non-breakthrough cases. Overall, immunized and non-immunized infants had similar rates of PICU admission and length of hospital stay. After age stratification and multivariable analyses, no significant association was found between nirsevimab immunization and severe outcomes. These findings suggest that nirsevimab may offer limited additional protection once hospitalization is required. The study provides insights into the real-world effectiveness of nirsevimab in preventing severe RSV disease and may guide future research and public health strategies for RSV prophylaxis.

title: Enhanced respiratory syncytial virus surveillance of young children admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, 2019-2023.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to comprehensively describe the clinical characteristics, management and outcomes of children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, determine the full burden of severe disease and identify population-specific risk factors for intensive care unit (ICU) admission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multi-centre, retrospective cohort study conducted over 5 years at two tertiary paediatric hospitals in metropolitan New South Wales, Australia, before implementation of government-funded immunisation programs against RSV in children. Participants included children aged <2 years hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2023, comprising all ICU admitted and a random sample of non-ICU admitted patients.
analysis.methods: The study involved examining the characteristics and incidence rate of RSV hospitalisations and ICU admissions among children aged <2 years. Factors associated with higher odds of ICU admission were identified using multivariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: Over a 5-year period, 4414 children were hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV, of whom 11.3% (499/4414) were admitted to ICU. The median age was younger in the ICU cohort (n = 499) compared with the non-ICU sample (n = 1000; 3.3 vs 7.1 months, P < 0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that RSV immunisation programs are expected to substantially reduce the burden of hospitalisation among Australian children in their first year of life. They also noted that children who are Indigenous, were born prematurely or have heart disease are at greatest risk of severe disease and may benefit from extended preventative programs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted preventative programs for high-risk groups, such as Indigenous children, those born prematurely and those with cardiac disease, to reduce the burden of RSV hospitalisations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted before the implementation of government-funded immunisation programs, which may limit its ability to assess the impact of such programs. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the retrospective design and potential for unmeasured confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a multi-centre, retrospective cohort analysis of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalisations among children under two years of age in Sydney Children's Hospitals Network from 2019 to 2023. It found that 11.3% of RSV hospitalisations required ICU admission, with younger age, prematurity, Indigenous identity, and cardiac disease being significant risk factors. The results suggest that RSV immunisation programs could substantially reduce hospitalisation rates, particularly among high-risk groups. The study's moderate evidence strength is due to its retrospective design and potential for unmeasured confounding, which may limit the generalisability of findings.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of human metapneumovirus and potential impact of respiratory syncytial virus interventions in the United States.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the factors driving the seasonal dynamics of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in the United States, particularly in relation to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), as the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed laboratory-confirmed HMPV cases and age-specific emergency department visits across 10 US regions, using an age-stratified dynamic transmission model to assess spatiotemporal patterns and the influence of environmental variables and RSV on HMPV transmission rates.
analysis.methods: The researchers fitted an age-stratified dynamic transmission model to HMPV cases and emergency department visits, incorporating climate variables and RSV activity to assess HMPV transmission rates and patterns.
analysis.main_results: The models incorporating climate variables could not capture the timing of HMPV activity across all regions, but models including RSV activity could reproduce the biennial pattern of HMPV, with HMPV transmission reduced in the presence of RSV.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study showed that RSV activity is a key factor in the biennial pattern of HMPV, with RSV interventions unlikely to result in a substantial increase in HMPV activity despite reducing competition from RSV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform future seasonal forecasting and intervention strategies for HMPV, highlighting the importance of considering RSV activity in HMPV epidemiology.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's reliance on models and the potential for unmeasured confounders limit the strength of the evidence, but the findings are consistent with the observed biennial pattern of HMPV.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the spatiotemporal dynamics of HMPV in the US, finding that RSV activity is a key factor in HMPV's biennial pattern, with RSV interventions unlikely to significantly impact HMPV activity.

title: Infant RSV immunity study (IRIS): protocol for a prospective birth cohort in Vancouver, Canada examining how age at respiratory syncytial virus exposure affects how infants respond to the virus immunologically.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how age at first RSV exposure affects infants' immune responses and respiratory health, addressing a knowledge gap in RSV immunology and disease severity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective birth cohort of 300 healthy infants in British Columbia, Canada, followed from birth to age 3 years, was enrolled to examine the impact of age at RSV exposure on immunity and respiratory outcomes.
analysis.methods: Infants were enrolled in April–June or September–November to ensure they entered the peak RSV season at either more than 6 months or less than 6 months of age. They underwent symptom-triggered oropharyngeal nasal swabs, post-season RSV serology, and serial blood and stool samples to assess immune responses and clinical outcomes.
analysis.main_results: The study will identify how age at RSV exposure influences RSV-specific immunity and respiratory outcomes, with findings to be disseminated through publications, scientific meetings, and participant communication.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study aims to determine how immune development at the time of exposure shapes RSV-specific immunity and long-term respiratory health, providing novel insights into the relationship between age at exposure and immune response.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of RSV infection, as well as vaccination strategies and prevention of recurrent or persistent wheezing and asthma.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include its prospective design and the potential for seasonal and developmental influences on immune responses, which may limit generalisability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: The Infant RSV Immunity Study (IRIS) aims to determine how age at RSV exposure influences immune responses and respiratory outcomes in infants, addressing a knowledge gap in RSV immunology and disease severity. The study involves 300 healthy infants in British Columbia, Canada, followed from birth to age 3 years, with symptom-triggered oropharyngeal nasal swabs, post-season RSV serology, and serial blood and stool samples to assess immune responses and clinical outcomes.

title: Beyond Croup: A Phenotype-Based Perspective on Parainfluenza Virus Types in Children.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on human parainfluenza viruses (PIVs) and their role in causing respiratory infections in children, with an emphasis on the distinct clinical and epidemiological characteristics of PIV types. The central question is whether PIVs should be considered as a single disease entity or as separate pathogens with unique impacts on pediatric health.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It provides general background on PIVs and their clinical relevance, but does not report on study selection criteria or the number of studies included.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the four PIV types differ significantly in taxonomy, tropism, clinical syndrome, and severity. It highlights that PIV-1 is the most common cause of croup, PIV-2 can cause severe disease in children with underlying conditions, PIV-3 is associated with bronchiolitis and pneumonia in young infants, and PIV-4 is linked to lower respiratory tract disease and occasional neurologic complications.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that PIV-4 has been historically underrecognized due to limitations in viral culture techniques. It also identifies gaps in understanding the full spectrum of clinical manifestations and the role of immune responses in varying disease severity across PIV types.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for improved diagnostic tools, such as multiplex molecular diagnostics, to better identify PIV types and guide clinical management. It also suggests the importance of developing targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies, as no vaccine or antiviral is currently licensed for PIV infections.

analysis.summary_en: This review provides a phenotype-based perspective on human parainfluenza viruses (PIVs) in children, highlighting their distinct epidemiology, clinical features, and immune responses. It underscores the limitations of focusing solely on croup as a clinical manifestation and calls for a more nuanced understanding of PIV types. The review notes that PIV-1 drives biennial epidemics, PIV-2 can cause severe disease in vulnerable children, PIV-3 is associated with bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, and PIV-4 is linked to lower respiratory tract disease and rare neurologic complications. Despite the burden of PIV infections, no licensed vaccines or antivirals are available, and emerging therapies show promise. The authors stress the importance of recognizing these differences for improved pediatric care and the development of targeted interventions.

title: Generative AI-Designed Immunoglobulin Domain Antibodies (IgDAbs) Against the Fusion Protein as a Neutralizing Agent for Respiratory Syncytial Virus.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to rationally design, screen, and experimentally validate novel immunoglobulin domain antibodies (IgDAbs) targeting the site II epitope of the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion (F) protein using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) driven tools. The scientific/public-health problem is the need for efficient and cost-effective methods to discover neutralizing antibodies against RSV, which causes significant respiratory infections. The knowledge gap is the lack of rapid and cost-effective methods for discovering such antibodies. The rationale is to leverage GenAI to accelerate the discovery process.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A generative AI tool was employed to generate 250 novel IgDAb sequences optimized for RSV-F site II binding. Candidates were screened computationally using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations to select hit candidates. The study design involved using an E. coli expression system to produce and purify the selected IgDAbs. The population included the RSV-A2 (long strain) used for in vitro microneutralization assays.
analysis.methods: The selected IgDAbs were cloned and produced using an E. coli expression system. Purified IgDAbs were characterized for target specificity via ELISA and evaluated for functional viral inhibition using in vitro microneutralization assay against RSV A2 (long strain).
analysis.main_results: Computational screening narrowed the library to 05 structurally compatible hit IgDAb with predicted binding affinity. ELISA confirmed specific binding of purified IgDAbs to the RSV-F protein. In vitro microneutralization assays demonstrated neutralization of RSV A2 (long strain), with two 'lead' IgDAbs showing EC50 of 1.3 μg/mL and 3.5 μg/mL.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Combining generative AI sequence generation with an integrated in silico and in vitro screening cascade enables the rapid, cost-effective discovery of neutralizing nanobodies against RSV, offering a viable alternative to resource-intensive traditional antibody discovery workflows. The novelty lies in the use of GenAI to accelerate the discovery process.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new therapeutic strategies for RSV, which is a significant public health concern. The results suggest a potential for rapid and cost-effective discovery of neutralizing antibodies, which could be used in the treatment and prevention of RSV infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of a single RSV strain (RSV A2) for the in vitro neutralization assay, which may not generalize to other RSV strains. The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited sample size and the use of a single strain.

analysis.summary_en: This study used generative AI to design and screen novel immunoglobulin domain antibodies (IgDAbs) targeting RSV-F site II, which were then experimentally validated. Computational screening narrowed the library to five hit IgDAbs, and in vitro assays demonstrated neutralization of RSV A2 with two 'lead' IgDAbs showing EC50 values of 1.3 μg/mL and 3.5 μg/mL. The findings suggest a rapid and cost-effective method for discovering neutralizing antibodies against RSV, which could inform new therapeutic strategies.

title: Under pressure: lessons learnt from rapid implementation of the respiratory syncytial virus maternal vaccine and infant nirsevimab in Sydney, Australia.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to share lessons from the rapid implementation of RSV prevention products and present data on immunisation uptake for mothers and babies in two maternity hospitals. The research addresses the need for effective strategies to improve RSV vaccine and nirsevimab adoption in clinical settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the rollout of the RSV maternal vaccine and the injectable monoclonal antibody nirsevimab in two maternity hospitals within the Sydney Local Health District. It examined immunisation uptake over a period from February to September 2025.
analysis.methods: Deidentified summary data from electronic medical records were analysed descriptively as counts and proportions. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research was used to evaluate the rollout process.
analysis.main_results: RSV vaccination coverage in women giving birth in the two hospitals increased from 4% in the first month of rollout to 70-74% from June to September 2025. The number of live born babies requiring nirsevimab decreased as antenatal coverage improved. Among eligible newborns, 36% of families declined nirsevimab, with reasons for refusal not recorded. Documentation of RSV immunisation status improved during the rollout.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the importance of multidisciplinary engagement and clear messaging in the successful rollout of RSV prevention programs. The study highlights the challenges and strategies for integrating multiple immunisation products into routine clinical practice.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of future RSV prevention programs by emphasizing the need for coordinated efforts, clinician education, and systematic safeguards to ensure accurate implementation. They also provide insights into improving immunisation uptake and documentation in maternity settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on deidentified summary data and the absence of recorded reasons for nirsevimab refusal. The evidence is moderate, as it reflects real-world implementation challenges but lacks deeper causal analysis or control groups.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the rollout of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention products, including the maternal vaccine and the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab, in two maternity hospitals in Sydney, Australia. It reports that RSV vaccination coverage among mothers improved significantly from 4% in February 2025 to 70-74% by September 2025. The number of infants requiring nirsevimab decreased as maternal coverage increased, while 36% of eligible newborns declined the antibody without recorded reasons. The authors highlight the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration, clinician education, and integrating immunisation into medical workflows for successful program adoption. They note that while the rollout was effective, the study lacks detailed causal analysis and control groups, limiting the strength of the evidence to a moderate level.

title: Dissolving microneedle patches for needle-free and thermostable respiratory syncytial virus vaccination.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of acute lower respiratory tract disease, yet current prefusion F (preF)-based RSV vaccines depend on intramuscular injection and cold-chain distribution, limiting broad deployment.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Dissolving microneedle array patches (MAPs) offer a minimally invasive, needle-free, and potentially thermostable alternative to conventional vaccine delivery.
analysis.methods: Here, we developed dissolving microneedle array patches loaded with an engineered prefusion-stabilized RSV F antigen (CL073A) and evaluated their potential as a needle-free, thermostable, and potent RSV vaccination platform.
analysis.main_results: Following formulation screening, two lead CL073A-loaded MAPs (MAPs-CL073A) were identified that preserved antigenicity and mechanical performance and showed prolonged local antigen retention relative to intramuscular injection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: In mice, MAPs-CL073A elicited markedly enhanced and durable humoral immunity, inducing approximately five-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers than intramuscular immunization at a ten-fold lower antigen dose, demonstrating a pronounced dose-sparing effect.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: In cotton rats, MAPs-CL073A conferred robust protection against RSV challenge by reducing lung viral burden and pulmonary pathology, with the 10 μg regimen (F2-MAP) achieving near-complete protection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Furthermore, the patches fully retained antigen bioactivity and in vivo immunogenicity after 6 months of room-temperature storage.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a dissolving microneedle array patch (MAP) as a needle-free and thermostable platform for RSV vaccination. The researchers formulated and tested MAPs loaded with an engineered prefusion-stabilized RSV F antigen (CL073A) in mice and cotton rats. The results showed that the MAPs-CL073A formulation preserved antigenicity and mechanical performance, with prolonged local antigen retention compared to intramuscular injection. In mice, the patches induced five-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers at a ten-fold lower antigen dose, demonstrating a dose-sparing effect. In cotton rats, the 10 μg regimen (F2-MAP) provided near-complete protection against RSV challenge by reducing lung viral burden and pulmonary pathology. The patches retained antigen bioactivity and immunogenicity after six months of room-temperature storage. These findings highlight the potential of dissolving microneedle delivery to enhance the efficacy and deployability of RSV vaccines. The study's evidence is strong, as it directly evaluated the performance of the MAPs-CL073A formulation in relevant animal models, supporting its use as a promising vaccination strategy.

title: Predicting prolonged hospital stay in children hospitalised with respiratory syncytial virus infection: model development, internal validation and a calendar-year transportability assessment

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a model for predicting prolonged hospital stays in children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and assess its transportability across calendar years. RSV is the commonest cause of lower respiratory tract infection in young children, and length of stay dominates cost.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on children under 5 years admitted to general paediatric wards in Chengdu, China, with RSV confirmed by multiplex polymerase chain reaction, from 2023 to 2025. The study included 494 admissions, of which 476 were analysed (median age 20.0 months; 57.6% boys); 106 (22.3%) stayed ≥ 7 days.
analysis.methods: Fifteen admission variables were ranked using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with 300 bootstrap resamples. Retention required 95% selection frequency and stability across four specifications. Discrimination was assessed with 500-resample optimism correction, calibration by slope, intercept and Brier score against a constant-risk benchmark, and utility by decision curves.
analysis.main_results: Age (odds ratio 0.49 per 16.7 months, 95% CI 0.38–0.64), co-detection (1.73, 1.07–2.79) and lactate dehydrogenase (0.66 per 66.6 U/L, 0.51–0.86) were retained. The model had an AUC of 0.708 (0.653–0.760), optimism-corrected AUC of 0.687, slope of 1.00, and Brier score of 0.158.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The model identified three routine admission variables that predicted prolonged RSV stay with moderate discrimination, preserved across calendar years. However, absolute risk was not preserved and requires recalibration before use.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of tools for ruling out prolonged hospital stays in children with RSV infection, aiding in resource allocation and clinical decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited by its retrospective design and potential for bias. The model's risk estimates were overestimated when applied to 2025 data, and the Brier score exceeded the constant-risk benchmark until recalibration, indicating moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a model for predicting prolonged hospital stays in children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection using routine admission data and assess its transportability across calendar years. A retrospective cohort of 476 children under 5 years admitted to general paediatric wards in Chengdu, China, between 2023 and 2025 was used, with RSV confirmed by multiplex polymerase chain reaction. The model incorporated 15 admission variables, selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with bootstrap resampling. Three variables—age, co-detection, and lactate dehydrogenase—were retained, showing moderate discrimination (AUC 0.708). The model's performance was preserved across years, but absolute risk was overestimated, and the Brier score exceeded the constant-risk benchmark. The model is suitable for ruling out prolonged stays but not for escalation. The study's findings have implications for improving clinical decision-making and resource allocation in RSV management, though the model requires recalibration for accurate risk prediction.

title: Incidence, shedding, and transmission of common respiratory viruses: data from a prospective, longitudinal, household cohort study in the Gambia from March 2021-June 2022.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viruses are a major cause of morbidity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet little is known about their incidence, risk factors, and transmission dynamics in community settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a prospective household cohort study in a peri-urban region of the Gambia. Households with ≥5 members, including at least one adult and one child, were enrolled and followed for one year.
analysis.methods: Upper respiratory tract swabs were collected weekly, regardless of symptoms, and tested by RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2, seasonal coronaviruses, human rhinovirus (HRV), influenza A/B, RSV A/B, parainfluenza viruses 1-4, human metapneumovirus, and adenovirus. We estimated incidence, symptomatic fraction, shedding duration, and household secondary attack rates (SARs), and explored associations with virus type and demographic variables.
analysis.main_results: From 2 March 2021 to 13 June 2022, 349 participants from 52 households completed 14,421 scheduled and 129 unscheduled visits. Respiratory viruses were detected in 11.1% of visits (n = 1611), representing 1423 infection episodes. HRV was most common, infecting 86.5% of participants (2.4 infections per person-year). Children aged <5 and 5-17 years shed virus for longer than adults (p = 0.0005), with longer shedding durations seen for HRV and SARS-CoV-2. Overall, 88.4% of infections were asymptomatic, with the highest symptomatic proportions for SARS-CoV-2 (16.3%) and RSV (17.7%) (p = 0.03).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: A large burden of asymptomatic infections underlies the circulation of respiratory viruses within households, with key differences in incidence, shedding and transmission across viral species.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for respiratory viruses, particularly highlighting the role of asymptomatic infections in household transmission dynamics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in a single peri-urban region in the Gambia, limiting generalisability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on observational data and does not include experimental controls.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to compare the epidemiology of multiple respiratory viruses within households in the Gambia. A prospective household cohort study was conducted in a peri-urban region, enrolling households with ≥5 members, including at least one adult and one child, and following them for one year. Weekly upper respiratory tract swabs were collected and tested by RT-PCR for various viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The study found that respiratory viruses were detected in 11.1% of visits, with HRV being the most common. Children aged <5 and 5-17 years shed virus for longer than adults, and asymptomatic infections were prevalent, with the highest symptomatic proportions for SARS-CoV-2 and RSV. The mean household secondary attack rates for all viruses combined was 6.7%. The study highlights the significant role of asymptomatic infections in household transmission dynamics and the differences in incidence, shedding, and transmission across viral species. However, the study's findings are limited by its single-location setting and lack of experimental controls, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Subtype-specific differences in susceptibility to monoclonal antibodies and vaccines among contemporary RSV-A and RSV-B isolates

analysis.research_question_and_background: IMPORTANCE Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We analyzed the viral genome sequences of 133 RSV clinical samples collected during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 seasons and selected representative isolates for phenotypic testing.
analysis.methods: We selected four RSV-A and four RSV-B replication-competent, sequence-verified stocks and then assessed them for replication kinetics in vitro and neutralization sensitivity with a panel of F-targeting mAbs and polyclonal sera using a rabbit vaccination model.
analysis.main_results: In a rabbit vaccination model, RSV-A-only sera efficiently neutralized all RSV-A isolates and the RSV-B1 reference strain but showed diminished activity against contemporary RSV-B isolates.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Antigenic cartography revealed a separation of antibody responses by subtype: RSV-A isolates clustered together and aligned with lower neutralization by antibodies such as MPE8 and 101F, whereas RSV-B isolates formed a distinct cluster associated with higher mAb susceptibility.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: We observe that RSV-A isolates are slightly more resistant to neutralization by mAbs than RSV-B isolates and that a bivalent vaccine elicits broader neutralizing responses than the monovalent vaccine.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This study provides insights into how viral diversity may influence antibody-mediated protection and suggests that recent RSV-B isolates may respond differently from the laboratory-adapted strains commonly used in research, an important consideration for the design of next-generation vaccines and antibody therapeutics.

analysis.summary_en: IMPORTANCE Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections. We analyzed the viral genome sequences of 133 RSV clinical samples collected during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 seasons and selected representative isolates for phenotypic testing. We selected four RSV-A and four RSV-B replication-competent, sequence-verified stocks and then assessed them for replication kinetics in vitro and neutralization sensitivity with a panel of F-targeting mAbs and polyclonal sera using a rabbit vaccination model. In a rabbit vaccination model, RSV-A-only sera efficiently neutralized all RSV-A isolates and the RSV-B1 reference strain but showed diminished activity against contemporary RSV-B isolates. Antigenic cartography revealed a separation of antibody responses by subtype: RSV-A isolates clustered together and aligned with lower neutralization by antibodies such as MPE8 and 101F, whereas RSV-B isolates formed a distinct cluster associated with higher mAb susceptibility. We observe that RSV-A isolates are slightly more resistant to neutralization by mAbs than RSV-B isolates and that a bivalent vaccine elicits broader neutralizing responses than the monovalent vaccine. This study provides insights into how viral diversity may influence antibody-mediated protection and suggests that recent RSV-B isolates may respond differently from the laboratory-adapted strains commonly used in research, an important consideration for the design of next-generation vaccines and antibody therapeutics.

title: Forecasting Respiratory Syncytial Virus Activity Using Seasonal ARIMA Models: Evidence from CDC Weekly Surveillance Data

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) imposes seasonal operational pressure on paediatric care and hospital healthcare systems. This study evaluates whether weekly RSV test percent positivity data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System (NREVSS) can support short-term forecasting of RSV transmission activity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The national weekly surveillance dataset spanning 3 January 2015 to 27 June 2020 was analyzed with four forecasting approaches: seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA), non-seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), exponential smoothing (ETS), and a seasonal naive benchmark model.
analysis.methods: Model predictive performance was validated via a 52-week chronological holdout sample and rolling-origin forecasts for 1–4 week ahead horizons. Multiple evaluation metrics were adopted, including root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE), directional accuracy, and peak-timing error.
analysis.main_results: Exploratory time-series analyses verified prominent annual seasonality and short-term serial dependence embedded in RSV percent positivity time series. Among all candidate models, SARIMA yielded the smallest RMSE and MAE on the holdout dataset, and exhibited relatively robust performance as the forecast window extended.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The overall findings demonstrate that surveillance-driven SARIMA forecasting can facilitate early epidemic warning and advance healthcare resource planning.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides evidence that SARIMA models can be used to forecast RSV activity, which can inform healthcare resource planning and early warning systems for seasonal outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Nevertheless, further external validation using post-pandemic and regional RSV surveillance datasets is required, as the sample only covers the pre-pandemic and early coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) period.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the potential of using weekly RSV test percent positivity data from the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System (NREVSS) to forecast RSV transmission activity. The researchers analyzed four forecasting models: seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA), non-seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), exponential smoothing (ETS), and a seasonal naive benchmark model. They validated the models using a 52-week chronological holdout sample and rolling-origin forecasts for 1–4 week ahead horizons. The results showed that SARIMA performed best, with the smallest root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) on the holdout dataset, and maintained relatively robust performance as the forecast window extended. The study highlights the potential of surveillance-driven SARIMA forecasting to support early epidemic warning and healthcare resource planning. However, the authors note that further external validation using post-pandemic and regional RSV surveillance datasets is needed, as the current sample only covers the pre-pandemic and early coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) period. The findings suggest that SARIMA models could be valuable tools for predicting RSV activity, which may help in managing healthcare resources during seasonal outbreaks.

title: Respiratory syncytial virus in adults in Moscow (2024–2025) - a case series

analysis.research_question_and_background: The role of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in the development of severe infections and decompensation of chronic diseases in adults is often underestimated. The study aimed to highlight the under-recognized impact of RSV in adult populations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a case series presenting three clinical cases of RSV infection in adult patients identified during a prospective study of RSV prevalence among 1,544 patients with acute respiratory infection in Moscow during the epidemic season of 2024–2025.
analysis.methods: The study involved the identification of RSV cases through clinical evaluation and prospective data collection from patients with acute respiratory infection. The cases were analyzed for clinical manifestations, comorbidities, and outcomes.
analysis.main_results: The first case involved a severe exacerbation of asthma in a 73-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension, requiring hospitalization. The second case was RSV-associated pneumonia in a 39-year-old man without comorbidities, complicated by myocardial infarction on the second day of hospitalization and co-infection with coronavirus HKU-1. The third case was a prolonged course of RSV infection (acute tracheitis progressing to bronchitis) in a 75-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities, leading to decompensation of arterial hypertension.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that RSV can trigger exacerbations of chronic diseases and vascular events in adults, even in those without underlying risk factors. This case series provides novel insights into the diverse clinical presentations of RSV in adults.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings emphasize the need for improved recognition and management of RSV in adults, particularly in vulnerable populations, and suggest the importance of targeted surveillance and prevention strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its case series design, which may not capture the full spectrum of RSV infection in adults. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on clinical observations rather than controlled trials.

analysis.summary_en: This case series highlights the under-recognized role of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in adults, particularly in triggering severe exacerbations of chronic diseases and vascular events. Three clinical cases from Moscow during the 2024–2025 epidemic season illustrate the varied manifestations of RSV infection, including severe asthma exacerbation, RSV-associated pneumonia with myocardial infarction, and prolonged infection leading to decompensation of arterial hypertension. The study underscores the importance of improving RSV surveillance and management in adults, especially those with comorbidities. However, the case series design limits the generalizability of the findings, and the evidence is considered moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

title: Sendai virus, a candidate vaccine for the prevention of respiratory virus infections in children: a review

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viruses including human parainfluenza virus (hPIV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), pose serious, potentially lethal threats to humans, particularly infants and young children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: While maternal vaccines and monoclonal antibodies are advancing to provide transient protection against these viruses, licensed pediatric vaccines are not yet available.
analysis.methods: Methods To examine the potential of replication-competent Sendai virus and its recombinants as pediatric respiratory virus vaccines against hPIV, RSV and hMPV, we searched literature databases and evaluated both historical and contemporary published research.
analysis.main_results: SeV and SeV recombinant vaccines have been tested pre-clinically in a variety of animal models and in Phase I clinical studies.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Results highlight SeV as an attractive pediatric vaccine candidate.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Continued clinical testing of SeV may provide global relief from serious respiratory viral infections in infants and young children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations or evidence strength assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates Sendai virus (SeV) as a potential vaccine candidate for preventing serious respiratory viral infections in children, particularly against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The study highlights the pre-clinical and early clinical testing of SeV and its recombinants, demonstrating their ability to induce immune responses and offer protection against multiple pathogens. The findings suggest that SeV could be a promising vaccine for pediatric use, though the evidence is limited to early-phase studies and lacks detailed limitations or strength assessments. The review underscores the need for further clinical trials to validate SeV's efficacy and safety in this population.

title: Temporal dynamics of respiratory pathogens among adult SARI patients in Shanghai, 2019–2023: a multi-center longitudinal surveillance study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to explore the temporal patterns of common respiratory pathogens among adult SARI patients before, during, and after the pandemic, as the epidemiology of SARI was greatly reshaped by COVID-19, yet long-term shifts in multi-pathogen circulation remain poorly characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective multi-center observational study was conducted across seven sentinel hospitals in Shanghai, China, from 2019 to 2023, enrolling a total of 4738 hospitalized SARI patients aged ≥ 15 years.
analysis.methods: Hospitalized SARI patients were tested for 12 respiratory pathogens (22 subtypes) using real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).
analysis.main_results: The overall pathogen detection rate decreased from 30.26% in the pre-pandemic period (2019) to 16.50% during the pandemic (2020–2022), then rebounded to 20.07% in the post-pandemic period (2023) (P < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study established a novel classification of four distinct temporal trends, including a continuous increase for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for persistent multi-pathogen surveillance to guard against single-pathogen outbreaks and concurrent multi-pathogen epidemics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and comprehensive pathogen testing.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the temporal dynamics of respiratory pathogens among adult SARI patients in Shanghai from 2019 to 2023. It found that the overall pathogen detection rate decreased during the pandemic but rebounded in the post-pandemic period. A novel classification of four distinct temporal trends was established, with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) showing a continuous increase. The study underscores the importance of ongoing multi-pathogen surveillance to monitor and respond to changing epidemiological patterns. The evidence is strong due to the large sample size and comprehensive testing, but the observational design may limit the confidence in causal interpretations.

title: AS01E-adjuvanted RSV pre-F protein vaccine in adults with lung or kidney transplant: a phase 2b randomized trial.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Immunocompromised adults are at increased risk of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This multicountry, open-label phase 2b trial evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of the AS01E-adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) over 12 months in kidney or lung transplant recipients ≥18 years, randomized 1:1 to receive one (n = 131) or two doses 30–60 days apart (n = 130). A control group of non-immunocompromised adults ≥50 years (n = 125) received a single dose.
analysis.methods: The primary outcome was the mean geometric increase in RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers one month following a second adjuvanted RSVPreF3 dose relative to the first dose in transplant recipients. Secondary outcomes included assessment of the safety and immunogenicity of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in transplant recipients compared with the control group.
analysis.main_results: In transplant recipients receiving two doses, neutralizing titers against RSV-A and RSV-B were numerically higher one month post-dose 2 than post-dose 1 (mean geometric increases: 1.34 [95% CI: 1.20, 1.48] for RSV-A [n = 111] and 1.26 [95% CI: 1.14, 1.40] for RSV-B [n = 111]). A single dose was immunogenic in transplant recipients, but showed slower and generally lower initial neutralizing responses than in non-immunocompromised controls, specifically in individuals receiving mycophenolate. RSVPreF3-specific CD4 + T-cell frequencies increased after vaccination versus baseline in all groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Both doses of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and had a similar and acceptable safety profile. Overall, these results support a favorable benefit-risk profile of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in kidney and lung transplant recipients.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Humoral and cell-mediated immune responses remained above baseline for 12 months post-vaccination. These findings suggest that the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine may provide sustained protection in immunocompromised individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The authors report results from a randomized phase 2 trial showing that the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine was immunogenic and had an acceptable safety profile in lung and kidney transplant recipients, supporting a favorable benefit-risk profile. However, the study was open-label and the sample size was relatively small, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This phase 2b trial evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of the AS01E-adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine in lung and kidney transplant recipients. The vaccine was well tolerated and showed a favorable benefit-risk profile, with sustained immune responses for 12 months.

title: Vaccine profile of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in adults: prevention of RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and emerging evidence of potential cardiovascular and respiratory benefits.

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an important cause of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and hospitalization in older adults, individuals with certain chronic medical conditions, and immunocompromised patients. The review focuses on the vaccine profile of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in adults, specifically its prevention of RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and emerging evidence of potential cardiovascular and respiratory benefits.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on clinical trial data and real-world evidence. Robust clinical trial data showed an acceptable safety profile and demonstrated efficacy against RSV-LRTD, with exploratory post-hoc analyses suggesting reductions in RSV-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)/asthma exacerbations. These findings are reinforced by real-world evidence showing effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalizations, COPD/asthma exacerbations, and cardiovascular events.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 was the first RSV vaccine licensed for preventing RSV-LRTD in adults, with initial approvals in 2023 in the United States and Europe. The vaccine has shown efficacy against RSV-LRTD and has emerging evidence suggesting potential cardiovascular and respiratory benefits, including reductions in COPD/asthma exacerbations and effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalizations and cardiovascular events.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that while the clinical trial data supports the safety and efficacy of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 against RSV-LRTD, the exploratory post-hoc analyses suggesting reductions in COPD/asthma exacerbations and cardiovascular events are not definitive. The evidence for these broader benefits is still emerging and requires further validation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: RSV vaccination should be considered within an integrated routine care and preventive management strategy for older adults and individuals with chronic conditions, alongside other adult immunizations and health interventions. Addressing implementation barriers for adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and emphasizing its role in maintaining health and independence will be critical to enable widespread uptake and help protect patient health.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the vaccine profile of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in adults, focusing on its prevention of RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and emerging evidence of potential cardiovascular and respiratory benefits. RSV is a significant cause of LRTD and hospitalization in older adults, individuals with chronic conditions, and immunocompromised patients. Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 was the first RSV vaccine licensed for preventing RSV-LRTD in adults, with initial approvals in 2023 in the United States and Europe. Clinical trial data demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and efficacy against RSV-LRTD, with post-hoc analyses suggesting reductions in COPD/asthma exacerbations. Real-world evidence further supports its effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalizations and cardiovascular events. While the findings are promising, the evidence for broader benefits remains emerging and requires further validation. The review emphasizes the importance of integrating RSV vaccination into routine care and preventive strategies for high-risk populations, alongside addressing implementation barriers to promote widespread uptake.

title: The "ever-vaccinated" stock-flow bias in adult RSV vaccine policy evaluation: A methodological caution and a flow-based remedy.

analysis.scope_and_question: Adult respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines are recommended as a single dose without routine revaccination; cumulative “ever-vaccinated” coverage is therefore a stock variable rising mechanically each season.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Prior guidance implies this stock–flow distinction, yet no study has provided a portable, instrument-agnostic remedy or quantified this decomposition for the 2025–26 season.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Using weekly 2025–26 U.S. National Immunization Survey data, we decomposed cumulative coverage into a prior-season stock and current-season flow, approximating the stock by the season-opening estimate. As of the latest available 2025–26 data (week ending 2026–02-21; mid-season snapshot), 84.9% of coverage among adults 75+ (43.2%) and 82.9% among high-risk adults 50–74 (32.8%) was attributable to prior-season stock – only 15–17% reflected current-season behavior; this stock share is an empirical approximation, not an exact decomposition.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: In two exploratory region-level quasi-experiments, the flow metric showed no sustained uptake acceleration (all primary tests p ≥ .19; a transient early-season gap, p = .008 post hoc, did not persist); these underpowered analyses are illustrative only, not identified for the policy effect. As a mid-season snapshot, these figures are an upper bound on the end-of-season value; the conclusion that coverage is dominated by prior-season stock holds through the season.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: RSV policy evaluation should pre-specify current-season flow as the primary outcome and report the stock share as a strongly recommended diagnostic.

analysis.summary_en: This review highlights the methodological challenge of evaluating adult RSV vaccine policy using the "ever-vaccinated" stock variable, which accumulates mechanically without reflecting current-season vaccination behavior. The authors decomposed coverage into stock and flow components using 2025–26 U.S. National Immunization Survey data, finding that prior-season stock accounted for 84.9% of coverage among adults 75+ and 82.9% among high-risk adults 50–74. These findings suggest that stock metrics may obscure equity monitoring in vaccine policy. The review also notes that exploratory quasi-experiments showed no sustained uptake acceleration in the flow metric, indicating the need for more robust analyses. The authors propose that future RSV policy evaluations should prioritize current-season flow as the primary outcome and report the stock share as a diagnostic tool.

title: Respiratory Infections at Mass Gatherings: A Travel-Medicine Review with Hajj and Umrah as a Longitudinal Case Study.

analysis.scope_and_question: Mass gatherings combine international mobility with dense, repeated contact and can amplify respiratory infections across travel corridors. Respiratory risk is determined less by attendance alone than by contact intensity, duration, ventilation, vocalization, shared accommodation, traveler susceptibility, and pathogen circulation.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A focused narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and authoritative public-health guidance. Searches and project evidence synthesis prioritized publications from January 2021 to August 2026, with selected foundational sources. No meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Recent Hajj evidence confirms a substantial burden of respiratory symptoms and clinical consultations, but estimates vary because denominators range from volunteers and tested samples to healthcare encounters. Rhinovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and bacterial pneumonia remain important.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Heat, dust, air quality, fatigue, and differential access to protective infrastructure modify respiratory symptoms, severity, and care seeking. Comparative events share mechanisms but not directly transferable rates.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Syndromic, laboratory, event-based, genomic, and wastewater surveillance are complementary, not interchangeable. Layered vaccination, risk-based masking, ventilation and crowd-flow measures, prompt diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and explicit travel histories, can reduce respiratory morbidity while preserving denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and its role in respiratory infections at mass gatherings, using Hajj and Umrah as a longitudinal case study. It highlights that respiratory risk is influenced by factors such as contact intensity, duration, ventilation, and traveler susceptibility, rather than attendance alone. The evidence base includes a narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and public-health guidance, with a focus on publications from 2021 to 2026. Key findings indicate that RSV, along with other pathogens like influenza and SARS-CoV-2, remains significant in these settings. However, estimates of respiratory burden vary due to differing denominators. The review also notes that environmental factors such as heat and air quality can modify symptoms and care-seeking behavior. It concludes that surveillance methods should be complementary, not interchangeable, and that layered interventions like vaccination and antimicrobial stewardship can reduce respiratory morbidity. The review emphasizes the need for maintaining denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

title: Surveillance of adverse events following immunisation in Australia, 2024.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This report addresses the need to monitor adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) to ensure vaccine safety, particularly for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines. The study aimed to evaluate the safety profile of vaccines administered in 2024, with a focus on RSV-related adverse events.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a national surveillance report conducted in Australia during 2024, encompassing all vaccines administered in the country. It includes data from the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on adverse events reported across the population.
analysis.methods: AEFI data were collected through spontaneous reporting to the TGA and analysed continuously and annually to identify new safety concerns or changes in known safety issues. The analyses focused on the frequency and types of adverse events associated with vaccines, including RSV vaccines.
analysis.main_results: In 2024, there were 6,232 AEFI reports for vaccines administered, with RZV (Shingrix) associated with the highest number of reported AEFIs. The most frequently reported adverse events were medication errors, hypersensitivity, gastrointestinal nonspecific symptoms, pyrexia, and injection site reactions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the slight increase in AEFI reporting rates in 2024 was likely due to the introduction of the new recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) and the expansion of the eligible population for zoster vaccination. This finding highlights the importance of monitoring new vaccines for safety signals.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the ongoing surveillance of vaccine safety, particularly for RSV vaccines, and support the need for continued monitoring of adverse events to ensure public health safety and improve vaccine programs.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on spontaneous reporting, which may introduce bias and underreporting. The evidence is moderate as it relies on observational data rather than controlled experiments, and the interpretation is grounded in the observed trends.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports on adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) in Australia for all vaccines administered in 2024. It highlights that RZV (Shingrix) was associated with the highest number of AEFI reports, with medication errors, hypersensitivity, gastrointestinal symptoms, pyrexia, and injection site reactions being the most frequently reported. The authors suggest that the slight increase in AEFI rates compared to 2023 may be attributed to the introduction of RZV and the expanded eligible population for zoster vaccination. The findings underscore the importance of continuous vaccine safety monitoring and provide insights into the safety profile of RSV vaccines. However, the study's reliance on spontaneous reporting introduces potential biases, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength.

title: Immunogenicity of the Foldon trimerization domain and efforts to shield it.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the potential immunogenicity of the Foldon trimerization domain in vaccines and its impact on eliciting off-target antibody responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved engineered influenza HA proteins with N-glycosylation motif mutations in the Foldon domain and evaluated their immunogenicity in mice.
analysis.methods: The researchers used mass spectrometry to analyze N-glycosylation modifications and assessed antibody binding using monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies against the Foldon domain.
analysis.main_results: Two of the three COBRA HA Foldon mutant antigens showed reduced binding by anti-Foldon antibodies, but mice immunized with these mutants did not have a significant reduction in anti-Foldon antibody elicitation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that while N-glycosylation modifications may partially shield the Foldon domain, they do not significantly reduce its immunogenicity in a naïve setting.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results should inform the design of clinical trials for vaccines containing Foldon, highlighting the need to consider its immunogenicity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to mice and does not account for human immune responses, which may differ. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the immunogenicity of the Foldon trimerization domain in vaccines, focusing on its potential to elicit off-target antibody responses. The researchers engineered influenza HA proteins with N-glycosylation motif mutations in Foldon and evaluated their immunogenicity in mice. Mass spectrometry confirmed partial occupancy of N-glycosylation modifications at two of three intended sites, and antibody binding was assessed. Two of the three mutant antigens showed reduced binding by anti-Foldon antibodies, but mice immunized with these mutants did not have a significant reduction in anti-Foldon antibody elicitation. The results suggest that while N-glycosylation modifications may partially shield Foldon, they do not significantly reduce its immunogenicity in a naïve setting. These findings highlight the importance of considering Foldon's immunogenicity during vaccine development and clinical trials. The study is limited to mice and does not account for human immune responses, which may differ, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Genomic diversity of respiratory pathogens in clinical versus community surveillance: a comparative analysis of SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza viruses in Washington State

analysis.research_question_and_background: BackgroundGenomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples.
analysis.methods: MethodsIn this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health.
analysis.main_results: FindingsWe analyzed 538 RSV sequences collected between 2019 and 2021 (278 community, 260 clinical), 1506 influenza sequences (260 community, 1246 clinical) between 2019 and 2020, and 8660 SARS-CoV-2 sequences (5923 community, 2737 clinical) from 2020 to 2022.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: InterpretationSeasonal respiratory viruses had similar dynamics and diversity in clinical and community samples, whereas pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differed between settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Genomic surveillance programs should combine clinical and community sampling, particularly during pandemics in order to better capture viral diversity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares the genomic diversity of respiratory viruses between clinical and community samples in Washington State, focusing on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. The research question addresses the gap in understanding whether clinical sequences accurately represent community viral circulation. The study design involves a retrospective comparative genomic analysis using sequences from both clinical and community sources. Whole-genome sequencing was employed to assess clade proportions, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values. The main results show that RSV and influenza had similar clade proportions and diversity in both settings, while SARS-CoV-2 showed differences, with community samples having more frequent clades 21J and 21K, and clinical samples showing more diversity in sequence clusters. The authors interpret these findings as indicating that seasonal respiratory viruses have comparable dynamics in clinical and community settings, but pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differs significantly. The study suggests that genomic surveillance programs should integrate both clinical and community sampling, especially during pandemics, to capture full viral diversity. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study is based on abstract-only data and does not report specific limitations.

title: An enhanced electrochemiluminescence immunosensor based on PtCo/UiO-66-NH2@luminol for highly sensitive detection of recombinant RSV F protein.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a sensitive and reliable method for detecting recombinant RSV F protein, addressing the need for improved diagnostics to prevent and control RSV infections in infants and young children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A sandwich-type electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensor was developed for the detection of recombinant RSV F protein, using a glassy carbon electrode modified with gold nanoparticles and a multifunctional PtCo/UiO-66-NH2 nanocomposite.
analysis.methods: The biosensor was fabricated by sequentially assembling chitosan and an antibody on the gold nanoparticles, blocking with BSA, capturing RSV F protein, and introducing a probe with another antibody, all designed to achieve cascaded amplification of ECL signals.
analysis.main_results: The biosensor showed a good linear relationship with recombinant RSV F protein concentration in the range of 0.1 pg mL-1 to 10 ng mL-1, with a detection limit of 0.025 pg mL-1, and exhibited excellent stability, specificity, and reproducibility.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the biosensor as a sensitive and reliable platform for detecting recombinant RSV F protein, which may serve as a foundation for future clinical validation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of improved diagnostic tools for RSV, aiding in disease prevention and control, particularly in infants and young children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for further clinical validation and the focus on recombinant protein rather than native virus, which may limit generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a sensitive electrochemiluminescence biosensor for detecting recombinant RSV F protein, demonstrating excellent stability and reproducibility, with potential for clinical validation.

title: Hospital burden, clinical severity, and economic impact of respiratory viral infections in Spain: A population-based study using hospital data (2019-2023).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections are a major cause of hospitalization, morbidity, mortality, and healthcare resource use in Spain. Although influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) account for most of the healthcare burden, the contribution of other respiratory viruses has been less studied.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective population-based study was conducted using the Spanish Minimum Basic Data Set (CMBD), including hospitalizations with a diagnosis of respiratory viral infection between 2019 and 2023. A total of 154,753 hospitalizations were included (mean age: 39 years; 48.6% female).
analysis.methods: Influenza, RSV, adenovirus, metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, and rhinovirus were analyzed. The study used hospital data to assess the burden, clinical severity, and economic impact of these infections.
analysis.main_results: Influenza and RSV accounted for most hospitalizations and total costs. A marked reduction in hospitalizations was observed in 2021, followed by recovery in 2022-2023. RSV, metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus predominantly affected the pediatric population, whereas influenza and parainfluenza had a greater impact on older adults. Overall, 6.5% of patients required ICU admission and in-hospital mortality was 2.7%, highest for influenza (4.2%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that respiratory viral infections impose a substantial healthcare and economic burden, with variable impact according to virus type and age group. This study provides novel insights into the relative contributions of different respiratory viruses to hospitalization and cost.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform integrated surveillance, prevention, and healthcare planning strategies for respiratory viral infections, particularly highlighting the distinct impacts of influenza and RSV on different age groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on hospital data and may not capture all respiratory viral infections. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on retrospective analysis and does not include detailed laboratory or clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the hospital burden, clinical severity, and economic impact of respiratory viral infections in Spain from 2019 to 2023. It highlights that influenza and RSV account for most hospitalizations and costs, with notable variations in impact across age groups. The research underscores the need for targeted surveillance and prevention strategies. While the study provides valuable insights, its reliance on hospital data and retrospective analysis limits its depth, resulting in moderate confidence in the findings.

title: Three-Year Polymerase Chain Reaction-Based Surveillance of Respiratory Tract Infections in Adults and Seasonal Patterns.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study investigated the aetiological composition, seasonal variation and risk factors of adult respiratory tract infections in Ganzhou, Jiangxi Province, during 2023-2025.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A total of 8,493 adults (≥18 years) with respiratory symptoms were enrolled from a tertiary hospital during 2023-2025.
analysis.methods: Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal swabs were tested using multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panels targeting six categories of seven respiratory pathogens, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Data were analysed by univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: The overall pathogen detection rate was 4.14% (352/8,493), comprising 325 single infections (92.33%) and 27 mixed infections (7.67%). Among single infections, RSV (16.00%) predominated. Infections peaked in winter-spring (December-March). Age ≥65 years (OR = 2.35, 95% CI: 1.78-3.09), underlying diseases (OR = 2.41, 95% CI: 1.89-3.08) and emergency department admission (OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 1.24-2.01) were independent risk factors.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the seasonal patterns and risk factors associated with respiratory syncytial virus in adults, providing insights into its epidemiological behavior.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support seasonally targeted surveillance and prioritised vaccination, expanded diagnostic panels and early PCR-based diagnosis for adults aged ≥65 years and those with underlying diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single tertiary hospital and abstract-only evidence, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a three-year polymerase chain reaction-based surveillance of respiratory tract infections in adults in Ganzhou, Jiangxi Province, during 2023-2025. It aimed to understand the aetiological composition, seasonal variation and risk factors of these infections. The study enrolled 8,493 adults with respiratory symptoms and tested oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal swabs using multiplex real-time PCR panels targeting seven respiratory pathogens, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The overall pathogen detection rate was 4.14%, with RSV accounting for 16% of single infections. Infections peaked in winter-spring, and age ≥65 years, underlying diseases and emergency department admission were identified as independent risk factors. The findings suggest that RSV has a significant seasonal pattern and highlight the need for targeted surveillance and early diagnosis in high-risk groups. The study is based on abstract-only evidence and has moderate strength due to its observational design and limited scope.
